turns.prompt: Explain the roles of try, except, else and finally. If an exception is raised halfway through the try block, where does execution go next? If two except clauses could both match, which one runs? Does finally run if the try block executes return?
turns.answer: The try section contains code that may raise an exception, and the except blocks catch a matching exception type; the first except that matches (checked in the order they appear) is the one that runs. If an exception occurs part‑way through the try block, the remaining statements in that block are skipped and control jumps directly to the appropriate except clause, after which execution continues after the whole try‑except‑else‑finally construct. The else clause is executed only when the try block finishes without raising any exception. The finally clause is executed in every case—whether an exception was raised, a return statement was executed in the try or except, or the code ran normally—just before the function actually returns.

turns.prompt: A least-recently-used (LRU) cache with a fixed capacity is often built from a hash map plus a doubly linked list of entries ordered by last use. What does each part contribute? Walk through what happens on a cache hit for key k, and explain why both get and put can run in O(1) time on average.
turns.answer: The hash map gives us direct O(1) average access from a key to its node in the doubly‑linked list, so we can locate the entry without scanning. The doubly‑linked list maintains the recency order, with the most‑recently used node at the head and the least‑recently used at the tail for easy eviction. On a cache hit for key k, we use the map to fetch the node, unlink it by reconnecting its previous and next pointers, and then splice it back at the head, updating only a constant number of pointers. A put operation either updates an existing node (moving it to the head the same way) or creates a new node at the head and adds a map entry; if the capacity is exceeded we remove the tail node and delete its key from the map. Because each operation consists of a few hash‑lookups and pointer adjustments, both get and put run in O(1) average time.

grade.rationale: The candidate correctly explains the roles of both the hash map and the doubly linked list, describes the pointer-level move to the front on a cache hit, and explains why both operations run in O(1) average time, fully meeting the level-2 rubric criteria.

turns.prompt: In a binary min-heap stored in an array, where is the smallest element and where is the largest? What do inserting an item and removing the minimum cost, and why?
turns.answer: The smallest element in a binary min‑heap is always at the root, which is stored at index 0 of the array. The heap only guarantees the parent‑to‑child ordering, so the largest value can be anywhere in the leaf level – roughly the second half of the array – and must be found by scanning those elements (O(n)). To insert a new item we place it at the end of the array and then “sift‑up” along a single root‑to‑leaf path, which takes O(log n). To remove the minimum we replace the root with the last element and then “sift‑down” that element along one path, also O(log n). Simply reading the minimum without removal is O(1).

turns.prompt: Under READ COMMITTED, the default in PostgreSQL, a reporting transaction runs SELECT SUM(balance) FROM accounts twice. Between the two reads, another session deposits 500 into an account and commits. Can the two sums differ? Could the report ever see the deposit before it was committed? Which isolation level would make both reads agree?
turns.answer: Yes, under READ COMMITTED the two SUMs can be different because each statement sees the data that was committed just before it starts, so the second SELECT will include the 500‑dollar deposit (a non‑repeatable read). The report can never see the deposit before it is committed, since READ COMMITTED does not allow dirty reads.
